content.text: Solids have definite shape and size, but they can be stretched, compressed or bent by external forces. Elasticity is the property by which a body tends to regain its original size and shape after the applied force is removed. The deformation is elastic deformation. Putty and mud tend to remain deformed and are examples of plastic materials; this property is plasticity.

Knowledge of the elastic properties of steel, concrete and other materials is important in designing buildings, bridges, automobiles, ropeways, aircraft, artificial limbs and load-bearing structures. Material strength, stiffness, weight, cost and resistance to permanent deformation influence design.

When a deforming force acts on a body, an internal restoring force develops. Stress is the magnitude of restoring force per unit area. For a normal force F acting over cross-sectional area A, stress = F/A. Its SI unit is N m⁻², called pascal (Pa), and its dimensional formula is [M L⁻¹ T⁻²].

The chapter describes longitudinal stress (tensile or compressive), shearing stress and hydraulic stress. Tensile stress accompanies stretching; compressive stress accompanies shortening; shearing stress accompanies relative sideways displacement of layers; hydraulic stress arises when a fluid applies pressure perpendicular to a body's surface.
Longitudinal strain is the change in length ΔL divided by the original length L. It occurs when a body is stretched or compressed along its length. Strain is a ratio and has no unit or dimensions.

Shearing stress is the restoring force per unit area associated with tangential forces acting parallel to a surface. Shearing strain is the relative sideways displacement Δx of opposite faces divided by the height or length L. For small angular displacement θ, tan θ ≈ θ.
equations: Shearing strain = Δx/L = tan θ ≈ θ

content.text: A solid submerged in a fluid under high pressure experiences forces perpendicular to its surface at every point. This hydraulic stress compresses the body uniformly, changing its volume without changing its shape. Volume strain is the change in volume ΔV divided by original volume V.
Strain is a fractional change in a dimension, such as ΔL/L, Δx/L or ΔV/V. Since numerator and denominator have the same dimensions, strain has no SI unit and no dimensional formula.

For small deformations, stress is proportional to strain for many materials. The proportionality constant is called the modulus of elasticity. Hooke's law is empirical and is not valid for all materials or beyond the linear part of the stress–strain curve.

A test wire or cylinder is stretched by gradually increasing an applied force. The strain and corresponding stress (force per unit area) are measured and plotted. The curve describes how a material deforms as the load increases; curves differ between materials.
In the typical metal stress–strain curve, region O–A is linear. Hooke's law is obeyed in this region, and the body regains its original dimensions when the load is removed.

In region A–B, stress and strain are no longer proportional, although the material can still return to its original dimensions after unloading. Point B is the yield point or elastic limit, and the corresponding stress is the yield strength σᵧ.

When stress exceeds the yield strength, strain can increase rapidly. If the load is removed in this region, the body may not regain its original dimensions; nonzero strain remains even when stress becomes zero. This is called permanent set, and the deformation is plastic.

Point D on a typical stress–strain curve is the ultimate tensile strength σᵤ. Beyond D, additional strain can occur even with a reduced applied force, until fracture occurs at E. A material is described as brittle when ultimate-strength and fracture points are close, and ductile when they are far apart.

Elastomers such as rubber and aorta tissue can undergo large strains and still return to their original shape. Their elastic region can be large, but they may not obey Hooke's law over most of that region and may not have a well-defined plastic region.

The ratio of stress to the corresponding strain in the proportional region within the elastic limit is called the modulus of elasticity. It is characteristic of a material and helps describe its response to deforming forces.

Young's modulus Y is the ratio of tensile or compressive stress to longitudinal strain. It can also be expressed in terms of force, original length, cross-sectional area and change in length. Its SI unit is Pa, the same as stress.

A material with a large Young's modulus requires a large force to produce a small fractional change in length. The chapter notes that steel is more elastic in this sense than copper, brass and aluminium, and is useful in heavy-duty machines and structural designs.

A structural steel rod has radius 10 mm, length 1.0 m, and is stretched by a 100 kN force. With Young's modulus 2.0 × 10¹¹ N m⁻², the chapter obtains stress 3.18 × 10⁸ N m⁻², elongation 1.59 × 10⁻³ m (1.59 mm), and strain 1.59 × 10⁻³ (about 0.16%).

content.text: A copper wire of length 2.2 m and a steel wire of length 1.6 m, both 3.0 mm in diameter, are connected end-to-end and stretched with total elongation 0.70 mm. The source uses the same tension in both wires and Young's moduli 1.1 × 10¹¹ N m⁻² for copper and 2.0 × 10¹¹ N m⁻² for steel; it reports a load of about 1.8 × 10² N.

In the human-pyramid example, 220 kg of additional supported mass corresponds to 2156 N, shared equally by two thighbones. Using bone's Young's modulus 9.4 × 10⁹ N m⁻², length 0.5 m and radius 2.0 cm, the chapter calculates compression of each thighbone as 4.55 × 10⁻⁵ m and fractional decrease 0.0091%.

The shear modulus G, also called modulus of rigidity, is the ratio of shearing stress to shearing strain. It can be written using force, area, length and sideways displacement, or using small angular displacement. Its SI unit is Pa. For most materials, the chapter notes G ≈ Y/3.

For the lead slab example, a shearing force acts parallel to a narrow face while the lower edge is fixed. The chapter calculates applied stress as 1.8 × 10⁶ N m⁻² and uses lead's shear modulus 5.6 × 10⁹ N m⁻² to obtain upper-edge displacement 1.6 × 10⁻⁴ m (0.16 mm).

content.text: Bulk modulus B is the ratio of hydraulic stress to the magnitude of the corresponding volume strain. The chapter writes B = −p/(ΔV/V); the negative sign represents the decrease in volume when pressure increases. Its SI unit is Pa and its equilibrium value is positive.

Compressibility k is the reciprocal of bulk modulus. It measures fractional change in volume per unit increase in pressure. Solids are least compressible, liquids are more compressible, and gases are most compressible; the chapter states gases can be about a million times more compressible than solids.

The chapter attributes the low compressibility of solids to tight coupling between neighbouring atoms. Molecules in liquids are less strongly bound to neighbours, while gas molecules are very poorly coupled.

Young's modulus relates longitudinal stress to longitudinal strain and applies to solids. Shear modulus relates shearing stress to shearing strain and applies to solids. Bulk modulus relates hydraulic pressure to volume strain and applies to solids, liquids and gases.

Lateral strain is the strain perpendicular to the applied force. Poisson's ratio is the ratio of lateral strain to longitudinal strain in a stretched wire. It is dimensionless and depends on the material. The chapter gives values of 0.28–0.30 for steels and about 0.33 for aluminium alloys.

Work done in stretching a wire against interatomic forces is stored as elastic potential energy. For a wire of original length L and area A elongated by l, the chapter derives energy as one-half times Young's modulus times strain squared times the wire's volume, equivalently one-half stress × strain × volume.

content.text: To avoid permanent deformation, stress in a lifting rope should not exceed the yield strength. For load W = Mg, the required cross-sectional area satisfies A ≥ W/σᵧ. The chapter's 10-tonne mild-steel example gives a minimum area about 3.3 × 10⁻⁴ m² and recommends a thicker rope with radius about 3 cm after allowing a safety margin of about ten.

A beam supported near its ends and loaded at its centre sags by an amount that depends on load W, span length l, breadth b, depth d and Young's modulus Y. Increasing depth is more effective than increasing breadth in reducing bending, but a deep thin bar can buckle.

The commonly used I-shaped beam section provides a large load-bearing surface and sufficient depth to reduce bending while limiting weight and cost. The design is a compromise that also helps prevent buckling.

Pillars and columns support structures. The chapter contrasts a pillar with rounded ends, which supports less load, with one having distributed ends. Structural design must consider operating conditions, cost, material reliability and long-term use.

The chapter estimates a mountain-height limit by considering shear stress in rock. At the base, stress due to the weight of material is approximately hρg; equating this to a typical rock elastic limit of 30 × 10⁷ N m⁻² with density 3 × 10³ kg m⁻³ and g = 10 m s⁻² gives h ≈ 10 km.

Stress is restoring force per unit area; strain is fractional change in dimension. The three types of stress described are longitudinal (tensile or compressive), shearing and hydraulic. Strain is dimensionless.
For small deformations in many materials, stress is directly proportional to strain. For tension or compression, F/A = YΔL/L, where Y is Young's modulus.

metadata.topic: Summary: Hooke's law and Young's modulus

content.text: A pair of forces parallel to opposite faces can cause one face to move sideways relative to another. For this deformation, the chapter gives F/A = GΔx/L, where G is shear modulus.

Hydraulic pressure can change a body's volume without changing its shape. The chapter summary relates pressure, volume strain and bulk modulus; the sign convention depends on whether volume change is written as signed or absolute fractional change.
For a wire suspended from a ceiling and stretched by a weight F, the ceiling force is equal and opposite to the weight, but tension at a cross-section is F, not 2F. Therefore tensile stress is F/A.

content.text: Hooke's law applies only in the linear part of the stress–strain curve.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Points to ponder: limits of Hooke's law

content.text: Young's modulus and shear modulus apply to solids because solids have lengths and shapes. Bulk modulus applies to solids, liquids and gases because it describes volume change under uniform stress.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Points to ponder: which moduli apply to which states

content.text: In everyday language, a material that stretches more may be called more elastic, but the chapter says this is a misnomer. A material that stretches less under a given load has a larger Young's modulus and is considered more elastic in this context.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.topic: Points to ponder: elasticity and stiffness

content.text: A deforming force in one direction can produce strains in other directions. For a wire under longitudinal strain, lateral dimensions also change; Poisson's ratio describes the relationship between lateral and longitudinal strain.

The chapter states that stress is not a vector quantity because stress itself cannot be assigned a specific direction in the same way as force. Force acting on a portion of a body on a specified side of a section has a definite direction.

content.text: NCERT exercise 8.1: A steel wire of length 4.7 m and cross-sectional area 3.0 × 10⁻⁵ m² stretches by the same amount as a copper wire of length 3.5 m and cross-sectional area 4.0 × 10⁻⁵ m² under a given load. What is the ratio of the Young’s modulus of steel to that of copper?

NCERT exercise 8.2: Figure 8.9 shows the stress–strain curve for a given material. What are (a) Young’s modulus and (b) approximate yield strength for this material? The graph itself is not available as a separate extracted asset.

NCERT exercise 8.3: The stress–strain graphs for materials A and B are shown in Fig. 8.10, drawn to the same scale. (a) Which material has the greater Young’s modulus? (b) Which material is stronger? The graph itself is not available as a separate extracted asset.

NCERT exercise 8.4: Read the statements and state, with reasons, whether true or false: (a) The Young’s modulus of rubber is greater than that of steel. (b) The stretching of a coil is determined by its shear modulus.

NCERT exercise 8.5: Two wires of diameter 0.25 cm, one steel and the other brass, are loaded as shown in Fig. 8.11. The unloaded length of steel wire is 1.5 m and that of brass wire is 1.0 m. Compute the elongations of the steel and brass wires. The referenced loading diagram is not available as a separate extracted asset.

NCERT exercise 8.6: The edge of an aluminium cube is 10 cm long. One face is firmly fixed to a vertical wall. A mass of 100 kg is attached to the opposite face. The shear modulus of aluminium is 25 GPa. What is the vertical deflection of this face?

NCERT exercise 8.7: Four identical hollow cylindrical columns of mild steel support a structure of mass 50,000 kg. The inner and outer radii of each column are 30 cm and 60 cm. Assuming uniform load distribution, calculate the compressional strain of each column.

NCERT exercise 8.8: A piece of copper with rectangular cross-section 15.2 mm × 19.1 mm is pulled in tension with a force of 44,500 N, producing only elastic deformation. Calculate the resulting strain.
NCERT exercise 8.9: A steel cable of radius 1.5 cm supports a chairlift at a ski area. If the maximum stress is not to exceed 10⁸ N m⁻², what is the maximum load the cable can support?

NCERT exercise 8.10: A rigid bar of mass 15 kg is supported symmetrically by three wires, each 2.0 m long. The wires at each end are copper and the middle wire is iron. Determine the ratios of their diameters if each wire is to have the same tension.

NCERT exercise 8.11: A 14.5 kg mass is fastened to the end of a steel wire of unstretched length 1.0 m and whirled in a vertical circle with angular velocity 2 rev/s at the bottom. The wire’s cross-sectional area is 0.065 cm². Calculate its elongation when the mass is at the lowest point of its path.

NCERT exercise 8.12: Compute the bulk modulus of water from initial volume 100.0 litre, pressure increase 100.0 atm (1 atm = 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa), and final volume 100.5 litre. Compare water’s bulk modulus with air at constant temperature and explain why the ratio is large.
NCERT exercise 8.13: What is the density of water at a depth where pressure is 80.0 atm, given that its density at the surface is 1.03 × 10³ kg m⁻³?
NCERT exercise 8.14: Compute the fractional change in volume of a glass slab subjected to a hydraulic pressure of 10 atm.
NCERT exercise 8.15: Determine the volume contraction of a solid copper cube, 10 cm on an edge, when subjected to a hydraulic pressure of 7.0 × 10⁶ Pa.

NCERT exercise 8.16: How much should the pressure on one litre of water be changed to compress it by 0.10%? The PDF text includes an additional trailing fragment, “carry one quarter of the load,” whose context is unclear.
